metadata.title: Using machine learning algorithms to predict students' general self-efficacy in PISA 2018

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the publicly available PISA 2018 microdata, merging Student Questionnaire and Principal Questionnaire responses at the student–principal level, yielding 79 countries/regions in the candidate predictor set. The analytic sample is then restricted by listwise deletion for missingness on the five self-efficacy items (84,179 records removed), and missing predictor values are imputed using median substitution. The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) in the ML training/evaluation pipeline, and the ML models (XGBoost, Lasso) are implemented in Python/scikit-learn without any stated weight-aware estimation. Therefore, readers should treat the results as predictive associations in the cleaned/imputed sample rather than fully design-weighted population estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values (PVs) are not applicable because the dependent variable is self-efficacy derived from five Likert items via an IRT transformation (general self-efficacy score), not a PV-based cognitive achievement outcome. Missing data handling is partially described: the authors use listwise deletion for missingness on the five self-efficacy items and median imputation for missing predictor values; however, the paper does not describe any PV-specific missingness strategy because PVs are not part of the outcome construction.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample is restricted to students with complete responses on all five self-efficacy items from the PISA 2018 Student Questionnaire; rows with missing data on any of these five items were eliminated (listwise deletion), reducing the dataset to 527,825 records. After this restriction, missing predictor values are imputed by substituting median values. The study uses merged Student Questionnaire and Principal Questionnaire data linked at the student–principal level (multiple students per principal), and then constructs a final feature set of 256 predictors (including dummy variables for categorical predictors) for ML model training.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (Student Questionnaire + Principal Questionnaire), self-efficacy (general) score
main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost (test set): R² = 0.467; RMSE = 9.699; MAE = 7.219. Lasso (test set): R² = 0.417; RMSE = 10.137; MAE = 7.683.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (Student Questionnaire + Principal Questionnaire) the study leveraged mastery goal orientation, meaning of life, proud emotion, positive emotions, and learning aspiration to predict students’ self-efficacy (IRT-transformed continuous score), finding that XGBoost outperformed Lasso with test-set R² of 0.467 (vs. 0.417). This indicates that affective and motivational constructs—measured in PISA questionnaires—can be used in ML-based monitoring to identify students with lower self-efficacy for targeted support, though the cross-sectional design prevents causal pathway claims.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (Student Questionnaire + Principal Questionnaire), self-efficacy (general) score
main_findings.performance_metrics: Reduced model (top 14 predictors) R² = 0.436; full XGBoost model R² = 0.467; exclusion model (without top 14) R² = 0.328.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 the study leveraged a reduced set of the top 14 predictors (including mastery goal orientation, meaning of life, proud emotion, positive emotions, and parents’ emotional support) to predict self-efficacy, finding that the reduced model retained substantial explanatory power (R² = 0.436) and that removing these predictors still left nontrivial variance explained (exclusion model R² = 0.328). This indicates that education systems could implement feasible, parsimonious ML-based early-warning tools using a small subset of questionnaire variables, while recognizing that remaining (lower-importance) factors still contribute indirectly.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (Student Questionnaire + Principal Questionnaire), self-efficacy (general) score
main_findings.performance_metrics: Top-5 predictors by socio-ecological level reported (relative importance values in Table 3); individual-level level ranked highest overall and exosystem ranked lowest based on available predictors.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 the study leveraged parents’ emotional support, teacher instruction strategies, cooperation climate, admission criteria, and country/economy of origin to predict self-efficacy, finding that individual-level motivational/affective factors were most predictive overall while exosystem-level predictors were comparatively weaker. This indicates that interventions should prioritize proximal student affect and motivation (plus family and classroom supports) while also considering how institutional and macro-context factors may shape self-efficacy indirectly.

data.outcome_summary: The study predicts general self-efficacy using PISA 2018 microdata merged from the Student Questionnaire and Principal Questionnaire across 79 countries/regions, transforming five self-efficacy Likert items into a continuous IRT-based score. After listwise deletion for missingness on the five self-efficacy items (final N=527,825) and median imputation for missing predictors, the authors trained XGBoost and Lasso regression with nested 4-fold cross-validation and grid search. On the test set, XGBoost achieved R²=0.467 (RMSE=9.699; MAE=7.219), outperforming Lasso (R²=0.417; RMSE=10.137; MAE=7.683). The top 14 predictors explained 43.6% of variance in self-efficacy, while excluding them reduced R² to 0.328. Because the design is cross-sectional and the paper does not report design-weighted estimation, results should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than causal effects.
